newsitem.title: UK: Britain launches supercomputer to probe cosmos.
newsitem.headline: Britain launches supercomputer to probe cosmos.

text.p: CAMBRIDGE, England (Reuter) May 19 - Britain on Monday launched a supercomputer powerful enough to turn scientists into "grand masters" of the universe.
The two million pound ($3 million) COSMOS is the country's first national supercomputer dedicated to cosmological research.
It will allow scientists to test their theories about the origin of matter and the structure of the universe.

Renowned physicist Stephen Hawking said during a lecture to mark the launch at Cambridge University that this was an exciting time in cosmology and COSMOS would help scientists test their theories about the origins of the universe.

Speaking through a speech synthesizer, the author of the top-selling A Brief History in Time, who suffers from cerebral palsy and is confined to a wheelchair said: "The calculations involved are so enormous they require a state-of-the-art machine."
COSMOS, made by California-based Silicon Graphics, will be used by the UK Computational Cosmology Consortium, a group of Britain's leading cosmology researchers.

The supercomputer at Cambridge University will enable British scientists to model the history of the universe from the first fractions of a second after its origins in the Big Bang, right through to the present day, some 15 billion years later.
Paul Shellard, director of UK-CCC, described Hawking and COSMOS as the two of the greatest minds at Cambridge.
He explained that scientists make models of the universe to test their theories. "COSMOS will allow us to take ideas and turn them into concrete predictions."
Among the theories scientists will test with COSMOS are how did the structure of the universe form, how did galaxies form and how did the universe begin.
"Computers like COSMOS can evolve their (scientists') model universes in exquisite detail and allow them to compare them with real world data," said Professor Neil Turok of Cambridge.
The university's Vice Chancellor, Alec Broers, described COSMOS which contains 32 high performance R10000 processors and 8,000 Mbytes of main memory, as the Deep Blue of cosmology.
But he said it was more sophisticated than the supercomputer that defeated chess master Gary Kasparov.
"It will go a long way to making us grand masters of cosmology," he said.
Turok told journalists that he and other cosmologists believe they are entering a golden age of their science and that COSMOS will help them achieve their ultimate aim.
"Our overall goal is no less than to crack the code of the universe," he said.
